about: The goals of the pipeline, as numbers (SLO = service level objective: a goal for the service that a test can measure). make scale-test (Step 6) and make drill (Step 7) measure them and say met or not met. Change a number here (make goals) and run make scale-report or make drill-report: the saved test is judged again, the measurements stay the same. Each goal says which test measures it (the field test): make scale-test measures the ones marked scale-test, make drill the ones marked drill.

objectives.text: The REST API answers (HTTP 200) when it is asked, also while the pipeline is under full load
objectives.why: The REST API is the part that a person uses. 99 percent allows a hiccup of the internet now and then (one call in a hundred), but not a service that is down.

objectives.text: The REST API answers quickly, measured from your computer over the internet
objectives.unit: milliseconds, for 95 percent of the answers
objectives.why: Past one second a person who waits for an answer thinks that something is broken. The number includes the trip over the internet (a new HTTPS connection every time costs about 0.1 to 0.3 s), so the REST API itself has about 0.7 s.

objectives.text: A new event can be read from the REST API soon after Kafka has stored it, with one producer and with the autoscaler at its maximum
objectives.why: The pipeline exists so that an alert can be read soon after the traffic happened. A minute is soon enough for a person who looks at an alert; a system that must react by itself would need a much smaller number and a different design.

objectives.text: After the load stops, the processors catch up: the backlog in Kafka is below 1,000 messages
objectives.unit: seconds after the load was switched off
objectives.why: A backlog is a debt: events wait for their turn. If the processors need an hour to catch up after every burst, the pipeline is as good as down for that hour.

objectives.text: With the load on, the producers' autoscaler has all its pods ready
objectives.unit: seconds after the autoscaler was freed
objectives.why: An autoscaler that needs ten minutes to react is no help against a burst that lasts five.

objectives.text: After the load stops, the producers are back to the minimum of 1 pod
objectives.unit: seconds after the load was switched off
objectives.why: Pods that stand idle still use CPU and memory on small machines that are paid for by the hour.

objectives.text: After the load stops, the processors are back to the minimum of 1 pod
objectives.unit: seconds after the load was switched off
objectives.why: The processors shrink only after the backlog is gone (while they work, their CPU is high); then their autoscaler waits 60 seconds and removes one pod every 30 seconds.

objectives.text: A pod that is deleted is replaced by a new pod that is ready, in every tier
objectives.unit: seconds after the delete, for the slowest of the five tiers
objectives.why: Kubernetes starts a replacement at once, but a pod needs time to start: Kafka and MongoDB need the longest. Two and a half minutes is a first guess for the slowest tier; the first real drill shows the real numbers, and this goal is then set from them.

objectives.text: After the delete, every part of the stack has its pods ready again (not only the replaced pod)
objectives.unit: seconds after the delete, for the slowest of the five tiers
objectives.why: The parts wait for each other: the REST API pods wait for MongoDB and the processor waits for MongoDB and Kafka. Five minutes is a first guess for the slowest tier; set it from the first real drill.

objectives.text: An event that is sent while a pod is being replaced is not lost: it can be read from the REST API afterwards
objectives.unit: seconds after the delete, for the slowest of the five tiers
objectives.why: The event waits in Kafka (or, while Kafka is gone, in the Job that sends it) and arrives after the recovery. Five minutes is a first guess for the slowest tier (Kafka: the producer has to wait for the broker); set it from the first real drill.

objectives.text: Deleting a pod deletes no data: every tier still has all the records and messages it had
objectives.why: The disks of Kafka and MongoDB belong to the StatefulSets, not to the pods, so a new pod gets the same disk. A pipeline that loses data when a pod dies is not a pipeline; 100 percent is the only acceptable number.

objectives.text: While one of the two REST API pods is replaced, the REST API keeps answering the calls for /stats
objectives.unit: seconds in a row without a good answer
objectives.why: The REST API runs as two pods so that one can be replaced while the other answers. Up to 5 seconds allows for the moment in which a call is still sent to the pod that is going away; a longer gap would mean that the second pod did not carry the load.
